props.title: Le Divorce

sections.content: **Le Divorce** (2003) exemplifies the sophisticated cultural clash comedy that dominated art house cinema in the early 2000s. Like **Lost in Translation** (2003) and **Under the Tuscan Sun** (2003), it explores American women finding themselves in foreign cultures, but with distinctly French flair. Director James Ivory brings his signature attention to social manners and class distinctions that defined earlier works like **Howards End** (1992) and **The Remains of the Day** (1993). The film cleverly uses an impending divorce between a French man and American woman as a lens to examine broader Franco-American cultural differences.

sections.content: The film sits within a rich tradition of Americans-in-Paris narratives, following the path carved by classics like **An American in Paris** (1951) and **Funny Face** (1957). However, **Le Divorce** takes a more nuanced approach to cultural differences, particularly around marriage, family, and infidelity. Kate Hudson's performance as Isabel Walker captures the wide-eyed American abroad archetype while adding layers of complexity as she navigates French social codes and sexual politics. SUBHEAD: Modern Paris Through American Eyes

Like **Midnight in Paris** (2011) and **Julie & Julia** (2009), **Le Divorce** uses its Parisian setting as more than just glamorous backdrop. The city becomes a character itself, with the film exploring both tourist landmarks and intimate local spaces. The treatment of food, fashion, and social etiquette reveals deep cultural differences, while the Kelly bag subplot cleverly illustrates how Americans and French assign different values to material objects and tradition.
